utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, of the Defence, and all those who are in the courtroom and outside. This will be our last working day this week, since it's a holiday tomorrow, and we will continue to examine the documents we started to deal with at the beginning of the week. This hearing will deal with the examination of about 50 documents, as suggested by the Defence. And as the Defence has put it, these documents will illustrate the problems encountered and it should show why the documents shouldn't be admitted. So as not to waste any time, we will follow the following procedure: The Defence will present its arguments on the basis of the list it has compiled. We will start with the first document. The first document having been dealt with, the Prosecution will comment on the Defence's position. There are about 50 documents. We have about four hours, if we deduct the pauses. So if we have 50 documents, we've got about five minutes per document. That's not much. Which means that both parties will have to be as concise as possible. Otherwise, we will not be able to move forward, and we won't be able to deal with the 50 documents. It would be best to conclude this matter because next week we're starting with an expert witness, and it's not really necessary to have a decision to deal with the documents, but we need to know what the final positions of both parties are with regard to the documents. Could the Defence start with the first document on the list now. Mr. Withopf, I am listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if you please allow me to make a few remarks and to address four distinct issues. Three out of them are linked to the discussion of the documents. But first we wish to hand over the proper, legible copies of the materials we handed over on Tuesday. And again, my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: My learned friend from the Kubura Defence, Mr. Dixon, quite correctly yesterday drew the attention of the Trial Chamber to Prosecution's Exhibit Number 125 on the further detailed consolidated exhibit list. This is the prior testimony of Mr. Robert Stewart in the Kordic case. For the record, the Prosecution removes this document from its exhibit list. It was an oversight on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The next issue, Mr. President, Your Honours, has to do with the list of the Defence for the accused Hadzihasanovic which details 36 documents to be discussed today. There are two distinct issues I wish to raise: Number one, on this list under numbers 193 and 198 appear two documents which were not contested by the Defence. These two documents are already in evidence. They were tendered by the decision of the Trial Chamber and they were assigned the Prosecution exhibit numbers P210 and P215. Accordingly, the Prosecution is of the view that we don't need to discuss them, including for legal reasons, not by way of example, since it would be a discussion of evidence, and this is not the right point in time to discuss the evidence. There is -- there are two additional or two further documents on the list for the Hadzihasanovic Defence. On the list appear the documents numbered 360 and 411. If one has a look at the Prosecution's further detailed consolidated exhibit list filed on the 19th of April this year, one sees immediately that these two documents have been removed. This implies, Mr. President, Your Honours, that they are not on the court records any more and therefore can't be discussed legally; they are not existent to these proceedings. There are two further issues I wish to address: There's one document due to an oversight is not -- or are not yet available in its original. It's number 59 on the contested exhibit list. We are making efforts to get this document or the original of the document in the course of the today's proceedings. And there's one last issue I wish to briefly raise in order to safeguard a smooth running of the today's proceedings, taking into account that we have to deal with the originals of the documents. Most of the documents to be discussed today, Mr. President, Your Honours, stem from the Sarajevo collection and therefore are the originals. They are currently signed out from the Evidence Unit under my name. I'm legally the custodian of these documents. They are accompanied by the ERF, what's the evidence register form. I suggest to keep the ERF together with the document to ensure that the document themselves and the ERFs don't get messed up. For the same reason, I have attached to each of the documents a little yellow marker. For the very same reason, I suggest that I hand over each original of the documents separately. They have to be shown to the Defence and the accused anyway, and in respect to some of the documents I wish to make comments obviously prior to hand them over. And a very last issue in this context - and this concludes my preliminary remarks - if the Trial Chamber would be inclined or would decide that they want to keep the originals of the documents, if they leave the court today - for example, for deliberations on the documents - one of the Judges has to sign the ERF to safeguard the chain of custody. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've listened carefully to what you have said. Apparently on the list of documents produced by Mr. Bourgon there are four that don't need to be referred to, so since there are two documents that have been admitted and haven't been contested - it's 193 and 198, those are the reference, and there are two others that were mentioned - and they're not necessary because the Prosecution has withdrawn them. So we have 32 documents remaining. In order to ensure that we deal with this as best as possible, I think the usher should take the original, give it to the Defence, show it to the Defence, the document will then be given to the Chamber before the Prosecution responds. The usher will then be given the original by Mr. Withopf. She will give the original to the Defence and to the accused and we will be given the document, which we will return to Mr. Withopf. If we need any originals, we'll deal with that later. Madam Usher, could you take the first document. It's number 8. Show it to the Defence, to the accused, and then show it to the Chamber. And during that time Mr. Bourgon will take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. The Defence can confirm what the Prosecution has just said; that is to say, there are four documents with erroneous numbers. We had some difficulties when trying to establish a link between the Prosecution's numbers for the contested documents and the -- the Prosecutor's PT numbers and the old Prosecution numbers, the internal numbers. So for these reasons the four documents in question are not the right ones. Nevertheless, I have the right numbers for these documents. It was a printing error. The right numbers are as follows: If we use the Prosecutor's internal list, the first number is 88, the PT number is 91; the second document is 92, the internal number is PT1465 -- 1465; the third document has the Prosecutor's internal number 257, and the PT number is 483; the fourth document, Mr. President, on the internal list is 826, and the PT number, 1451. When I deal with these documents, we will also have the numbers that are contested documents on the list of contested documents. Without further delay, Mr. President, I will now turn to the first document. The first document is number 2 on the list of contested documents; the Prosecution's list, the internal number, is 8 and the PT number is 8. With regard to this document, Mr. President, the first thing that we had a look at in the case of each document was the signature. If you have a look at this document, Mr. President, there is no signature. It has not been signed. Then if we want to see whether the document was received by anyone, we are not in a position to establish this. We don't know whether it was received by anyone. There is a stamp, which is at the top of the document. On the first page of the original document, we have a stamp which gives us a date. The 11th of December, 1992 is the date. And there is also a reference. There is a code number. But we do not know whether this document was received or sent. But in the translation of the document, on the first page of the English translation it says: "Received on the 11th of December, 1992." When we have a look -- when we try to see who the document was sent to, the translation says that the document was apparently sent to Vitez OBSO. We don't know what that is. And also to the 325th Mountain Brigade. And it is not clear when looking at this document -- we don't know what happened with the document. As I said at the beginning, the document hasn't been signed, and there is the printed name of the accused, the commander, General Hadzihasanovic. On the basis of the original that I've been provided with - it's the first time I see it - this is probably a document that was sent in electronic form. So as has already been explained by the Chamber, sometimes colours can help us. When I have a look at the original, I can see that there is no original stamp, or perhaps there is a stamp on the back. It's difficult to see. But it concerns the accused directly. When we have a look at the contents of the documents, this is a document addressed to all units and it tells the units in some sense these are the tasks that you have to carry out on the basis of the situation on the 10th of December, 1992. We don't know whether the units received this document. All we know is that there is a stamp. And even if we accept that this stamp shows that it was received - because the colour is different - we don't know who this document was received by. On the document itself, it says something in handwriting. It says "OPSO Vitez" and the "325th." Does this correspond to the document sent or received? We don't know. A little further down you can see the letter "K" on the second page of the original. It says "325," which must refer to the 325th Brigade. And that number has been circled. Was it circled when the document was sent or when the document was received? These are things we do not know. So this is one of the categories of documents, Mr. President, which in our opinion render the Trial Chamber's task too difficult. So without additional support, it would be too difficult for the Chamber to admit this document into evidence. There are too many difficulties that would -- for the Trial Chamber to be able to use this document and consider it to be reliable. We know that the document exists on the basis of the proof we received yesterday. We know that the document arrived in the archives. But we do not know whether the document remained in the 3rd Corps or whether it went anywhere else or whether anyone received this information. That concerns the first document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you show the document to the two accused so that they can examine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, I should like to make an additional remark regarding this document, and this is a detail that applies to almost all the documents that we will see this morning. If we look at the document, Mr. President, the translation - I refer to paragraph 2 and subparagraph (a) - there's mention of the 318th BBR, so it's probably a brigade from Zavidovici. Then we see the letters O-P-S-O, OPSO, and in brackets "without the 1st PDO". What I wanted to underline is that you have a brackets and an interpretation by someone - I don't know if it's someone in the translation service of the Prosecution or some other person - an interpretation of the PDO letters as "anti-sabotage detachment." In several places within this document, Mr. President, you have references within brackets, and these are interpretations or details that have been added. Perhaps my learned friend could explain whether the information within the brackets was provided by the translation service or by the Prosecution, because this is an addition to the document and it actually specifies what is in the document or which may not be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution. The Chamber has the document in its possession. There was another remark that you could have made that you didn't, and that is that this document consists of several pages, and one can see that one can cut the pages, and this is obviously a document coming from a fax on a rolling -- on a roll of paper, and that this document probably followed a series of documents that were transmitted at a given point in time, because one can see clearly that it was cut at the bottom and also at the top, so it must have been part of a roll of documents that was being faxed. And Mr. Bourgon, who was a military man, could have told us that. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I note that my learned friend from the Defence talked about six and a half minutes of this document, more than the time that was allocated for both parties. If I may please address a few of the issues. First of all, in respect to the authenticity of this document, this is an official document of the ABiH, as one can see from the original, and it stems from the Sarajevo collection 1. The relevance as outlined in the pre-trial brief, deployment of troops in respect to the crime base in Dusina. Rule 89(D), it's from the Sarajevo 1 collection, there are no irregularities in obtaining this document, and it has been disclosed in time. There are a number of technical issues my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence has addressed and factually they are correct. There's no doubt about this. The fact that this document doesn't bear a signature can easily be explained because, as Your Honour the Presiding Judge already mentioned, this is a document which was sent. And as it is obvious from the document, it was sent electronically, and therefore the document doesn't have a signature. Pretty straightforward explanation, and it's correct; there are other such documents as well. The second issue which my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence has addressed: There are -- and that's correct. There are in brackets explanations. These explanations - and the one which has been addressed by my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence, under 2(a) - there is after the word "PDO", or after the abbreviation "PDO" there is a question mark and then there is "anti-sabotage detachment." Such explanations are made by CLSS. They are by no way made by the Prosecution. CLSS -- and CLSS is not part of the Prosecution. I wish to mention this. CLSS has people who are very qualified and they are in a position to explain what certain abbreviations do mean. They, however, identify if they are not sure such portions with a question mark. This only serves for the purpose to have the best knowledge of the document possible, and it's very common. This is the very same issue in all proceedings before Trial Chambers of the International Criminal Tribunal. All such documents -- or quite a number of such documents have such additional explanations. It's obviously common. This document, Mr. President, Your Honours, as many other documents to follow, illustrate that this is not an issue about admissibility. For the reasons my learned friend has mentioned, one may or may not be inclined to attach less probative value to the document, but it's not - and I wish to emphasise this - it's not an issue of not admitting this document. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber has listened carefully to what you told us. As far as I'm concerned, I should like to indicate that the remarks of the Defence were relevant regarding the reference to the addition of anti-sabotage unit. You explained that it is the translators who do that. In theory, in countries of continental law, when there's a translation, the translation has to be faithful, and it may be accompanied with another document coming from the translator, a kind of dictionary, with the translator saying that the abbreviation "PDO" is the equivalent of an anti-sabotage unit. But that's another document. The judicial translation of a document should not contain any personal judgement on the part of the translator. This is a technical matter that is very well known. I assume the same applies to Canada and the United States. You will tell me that that is the established practice. It is true that the Rules of Procedure make no mention of that. But if we wish to have judicial security, it would be better for the document to be translated in its integrity without any commentary by the translator, and then on an attachment the translator could explain that the abbreviations stand for such-and-such a thing. Let us move on to the next document, please. Madam Usher, we can give the first document back and we will see later whether we need it. Mr. Bourgon, you exceeded by 1 minute 30 seconds the time planned. If we had a sand clock, I would have to turn it around by now. But anyway, we will trust you that you will do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without further delay, let me go on to the next document. It is number 10 on the list of contested documents, 35 on the internal list, and 35 on the PT list. The document in question - I don't have the right document with me. This is not the proper original, Mr. President. It is document number 10 on the list of contested documents of the Prosecutor, 35 on the internal list, and 35 as the PT number. I don't know whether the Chamber has this document in its possession. It has the number "PT35" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this is correct. It's my fault. This is actually a war diary, and I'll hand it over now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question here with respect to this document is as follows: First of all, this is a handwritten document. The author is known -- is not known; the purpose is not known. The instructions given to him are not known, and also the date of the drafting of the document is not known. We don't know how and why this document was drafted. To be even more specific, Mr. President, my learned friend is giving me now the diary itself of the 3rd Corps in its entirety. It was one of our -- one of our main points with regard to this diary is the Prosecutor did have the whole diary. But the question is what the Chamber will have when it deliberates. The Chamber will have the whole diary or will the Chamber have only this document? It is a document drafted in hand without signature, without date, without any other indication. The only reference is "OG Bosna." And also, different handwritings are used on this same document. Therefore, if the Chamber were to use this document, it does not meet the criteria of reliability which would allow the Chamber to make any conclusions without saying to themselves, "Yes, but." And that's our whole point. Without any additional testimony, the document must at least speak for itself and tell the Chamber what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war diary that you have in front of you, have you had a copy of the whole war diary? Has it been disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know. We received this document, and we prepared ourselves on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know whether you had a copy. My second question: In the pre-trial phase and during the trial itself, you always could have gone and seen the originals as a Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. But in view of the fact that there are more than 100.000 pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's difficult, but your observation is quite correct. Madam Usher, please give the war diary to the accused to look at first, and then we can -- give it to us. Madam Usher, will you show the diary to Mr. Dixon, please. Mr. Withopf, while you are speaking, we can have a look at the war diary, so please begin. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Very briefly, in respect to the authenticity. This is an official document of the ABiH. It's a war diary of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, as the first page in this diary will show, and it stems from the Sarajevo collection 1. It's relevant. It's a 3rd Corps war diary covering portions of the indictment period. The entries from the 14th of March, 1993 [sic]. It's referenced to in the pre-trial brief, and it concerns the kidnapping of the witness Totic, and it will provide notice in respect to the accused Hadzihasanovic. In respect to Rule 89(D), in order to not waste time, I make reference to what I said to the first document. Technical issues. This is a war diary, and my learned friend has quite correctly mentioned that there are different handwritings in it. Each army has such war diaries and they are in handwriting, and they are in handwriting because the person who writes or makes entries into such a war diary is the duty officer or the duty soldier who receives information from external sources and writes it down in the diary. That's the whole purpose of such a diary. That can easy -- easily be explained. To my knowledge - however, I would have to confirm this - it's the understanding that the full war diary was disclosed -- or a copy of the full war diary was disclosed to Defence certainly in time. The date can be seen from the original of the war diary. The Prosecution is very well prepared if the Chamber deems it appropriate to tender a full copy of the full war diary. Mr. President, Your Honours, as Your Honour Mr. Presiding Judge already mentioned, Defence could have had a chance to have a look at the original of the war diary. For the information of the Trial Chamber, I wish to mention that at the early stages of the proceedings Defence requested to see the original maps. Defence obviously within a short time frame was given the opportunity to see the original maps. If they would have done so in respect to the war diary or any other originals, the Prosecution would have been in a position and would have been prepared to provide them access.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Mundis is taking my -- is drawing my attention to the fact that in the transcript it's written "14th of March, 1993." I think that's actually the right -- the right date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No, I think it's the 14th of March, 1993. It appears to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document, it says the 14th of May. I wanted to say that the war diary we have in our hands, the green colour, there's a big number and it says in B/C/S "Ratni Dnevnik" and I believe the translation is "war diary." Then there's a number 2. There must be a number 1 which we don't have. And also, it says the 13th of March, 1993 to the 14th of May, 1993. So the first handwritten entry begins the 11th of March, 1993, and the last -- the last document on the last page does not appear to have a date, but on the bottom it says the 14th of May, 1993 in black marker. This may be the archivist who made this note, because it says, "Listova 1997." And this may have been written by the archivist. So we don't know exactly. Do you have anything to add, Mr. Withopf? In any event, we see the stamp of the 3rd Corps on this document on the one-but-last page. I wish to show it to Mr. Bourgon. You see the stamp, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this junction, I have nothing to add. There will be a second war diary shown today. It will be of a very similar nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wish to give you this document back. Mr. Bourgon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Bourgon. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Number 12 on the internal list of the Prosecution, number 38 and PT number 38 as well. This document comes under the same category. So I will address myself to both documents. The position of the Defence has nothing to do with time. We didn't say that we didn't have enough time to prepare ourselves. The relevance is not in question either, Mr. President. The only thing that is in question is that we are of the opinion that the Chamber cannot use this document only without having the original document in its entirety. That is why we would like, Mr. President, that the Prosecution be asked to provide the war diary in its totality with the translation so that it is possible for the Chamber to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears that the accused are not hearing the interpretation. It may be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document number 38, document 12, where is the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is part of the very same war diary you had in your hands a few seconds ago, and it can be provided again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, the diary should be given again for Defence counsel to check page 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technical problem seems to apply to us as well. We are not getting the interpretation into the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar is telling us that someone is going to come in a minute to deal with it. But in order not to waste time, if Madam Usher can hear me, can she get the diary to give it to the Defence counsel so they can check page 46 in the original. [In English] It's okay? [Interpretation] Can everyone hear now? Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. In order to not waste time, there's not much to add, the Prosecution has offered to provide the Trial Chamber and to tender a full copy of the war diary if the Chamber feels it appropriate to do so. The date of this entry is obviously, as can be seen from the original, the 16th of April, 1993. It's relevant. It's referenced to in the pre-trial brief, and it shows the subordination and deployment of military troops of the 3rd Corps eight days prior to the killings in Miletici. Thank you very much. If I may add since this is obviously a very official document with the necessary stamps on it, it again shows that we are talking about the probative value only; we are not talking about the admissibility. And this applies to most, if not all, of the documents Defence wishes to discuss today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the date, the Chamber notes that after this document, there's another document marked the 17th of April, 1993 in a different handwriting, and that in this document, which is on page 46, there's a page 45, and on page 45 the date is the 16th of April, 1993. So the conclusion one could make quite easily is that this document was drafted on the 16th of April. So I am returning the document. Let us move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should simply like to add one comment regarding the last document. First of all, the way in which the document was given to the Defence. When we look at the numbers, the ERN numbers, we see that these documents were photocopied page by page and given to the Defence page by page. So it's quite possible that the document in its entirety was given to the Defence. But the whole Sarajevo collection was given to us on a CD-ROM, so the only way we had to look at the documents was to print 55.000 pages one by one or to search through them. And we didn't come across the diary as a whole. But during our search, we received pages like this. So the principal point of the Defence is always the same, and that is: Will the Chamber only have this document before itself -- before it to use or the whole document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The suggestion is that the totality of the war diary be tendered. Mr. Withopf, please, preserving your legendary calm, what is it that you wish to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: As my learned friend mentioned, the full diary has been disclosed and it has been disclosed on a searchable CD. If my learned friends from the Defence are not in a position to do searches, the Prosecution is certainly very well prepared to provide training in doing such searches. It's a matter of ten minutes to find out which pages are related to which war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we need to deal with the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do so, Mr. President, but the Defence believes that the Defence should tell the Trial Chamber that we do not appreciate the Prosecution's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, I was also going to say that you should carry on and remain calm, as usual. We understand the technical difficulties you have encountered. You have explained them to us. Going through 5.000 [as interpreted] pages is an immense task, and we do understand the difficulties that you are confronted with. So be aware that the Trial Chamber is aware of these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The following document has the number on the Prosecution's list 16, the internal number is 51, and the PT number is 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you fetch the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document, as you can see, needs to be consulted by looking at the last page. It's a handwritten page, a note which has been handwritten and signed in a language that is not one of the Tribunal's official languages. There is a date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document we have, under number 16 isn't a handwritten document; it's a typewritten document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document consists of three pages. First of all, we have a handwritten page, and then there is a typewritten page, and then we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not have the handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll give you the original, which we obtained from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The handwritten document wasn't admitted, no request made, because we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we don't have the handwritten document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a look at it, then. We will then show it to the accused, but we would just like to check the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two documents that are typewritten, the date of the 24th of October, 1993, and the original has 01502850; that's the number in red. The second document should be a copy of the original. We have the handwritten document that we didn't have. We now have it before us. This document is in English, and there is a signature in the Arabic script at the bottom -- at the end of the document. There is a reference to Allah in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will show it to the accused. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document was handwritten. This is the first document, the date of which is a date that's not used by the calendar used here. It's the 24th of the 10th month of the year 1413. This document was written in English. The original was written in English. We would like to point that out, Mr. President. And it was addressed to "to whom it may concern." We do not know to whom the document was addressed. The signature at the bottom of the document can't be identified on the basis of what we have before us, Mr. President. This document was then translated into B/C/S by someone we do not know, someone who didn't sign the document, and then added on the same document is something by another typewriter. There's a PS note and it says that this document was forwarded to someone from the HVO. We do not know this person's name, and the signature isn't contained in the document either. It's by someone called Merdan. According to the information that the Trial Chamber has, this would be the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. The arguments we have with regard to this document are as follows: There's a document that was perhaps drafted by a foreigner, but in any event, it's someone who speaks English. This document was forwarded to the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, who apparently forwarded it to an HVO member, who apparently had it translated and apparently had it placed in the archives. None of this was signed. The document then appears before the Chamber today with the new English translation. When we compare the two translations, the English translation of the B/C/S document, and when we compare this with the English original, we note that there are certain discrepancies. Our problem, Mr. President, today is that such a document needs additional support. There are three persons involved: There's the person who drafted the document, the person who apparently received it, and who apparently forwarded it to a third party. So we have Person A, B, and C. None of these persons signed this. We have no testimony of Person A, B, or C. So it is our opinion that we cannot attach any probative value to such a document. This document requires some form of support, if the Trial Chamber is to be able to use it for any purposes without having to speculate about what happened in relation to this document. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now let Mr. Withopf take the floor. But I would like to point out that in the handwritten document, which is obviously the original, there are certain things written in the Arabic script and it would have been good if an investigator who had some knowledge of penal procedure, it would have been good if these Arabic words had been translated. Perhaps it contains important information. We don't have a translation. In the English translation, it says: "Signature in Arabic" perhaps, but perhaps it's something else. This is something we do not know. Madam Usher, could you show these documents to the accused, and Mr. Withopf will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I note that my learned friend from the Defence in respect to this document talked about the probative value, and I certainly do agree that one can discuss about the probative value. My learned friend didn't address the issue of admissibility, and that's the gist of this whole debate. We were entering meanwhile into a discussion about probative value. The main purpose of our today's discussion is the issue of admissibility. Even if the probative value can be discussed, the admissibility is a different issue. In respect to this particular document, in respect to authenticity it's a document from the Croatian state archive. As I mentioned on Tuesday, the original the Prosecution has in its possession is actually a copy. It can be identified as a copy from the Croatian state archive having a look at the stamp at the top right-hand corner of the document. The document is obviously relevant. It addresses the exchange of foreign nationals against HVO prisoners handed over to Dzemal Merdan, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, and it's relevant to the subordination of the Mujahedin. The date which is, as my learned friend quite correctly emphasised, it's a date following the Islamic calendar; however, there's a fax transmission line at the very top of the document which identifies that this document was sent on the 25th of April, 1993. Again, the issue is of probative value, and I agree it can be discussed. But in respect to admissibility, the Prosecution is of the view that this document is admissible. It's correct that this document contains a very small portion of Arabic script and the translation says "Signature in Arabic." The Prosecution can make further inquiries whether it's possible to actually figure out what the Arabic letters do mean. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will move on to the next document. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, it is clear that the Prosecution will stand by its position and repeat in regard to each document the issue of relevance, even though we don't insist on this issue. The Prosecution will continue to talk about probative value. But it's clear that admissibility has to take into account probative value. We have discussed this issue over a two-day period. The Chamber is aware of the Defence's position and the Prosecution's position, and repeating these issues today is not useful. It's not relevant and it wastes the Trial Chamber's time. We quite simply want to discuss the documents, Mr. President. The last document has no probative value -- hasn't got enough probative value, in our opinion, in order for it to be reliable. My colleague said that we have a document from Bosnia and Herzegovina. He said it's an official document taken from the Croatian archives. How did a document end up in the archives -- how did a document from one country end up in the archives of another country? Were the archives stolen? How is it that a photocopy from the archives in Croatia can be an official document for another country? All these issues, Mr. President, are issues that we can raise. All we're trying to do today is to go through each document and to point out the shortcomings and deficiencies in each document and then the Trial Chamber can assess the matter. It's necessary to determine whether there is enough probative value to see whether a document can be used with additional support, and we need to take into account all the criteria, the translation, the reliability, authenticity, et cetera. This is how we will proceed with the next document, Mr. President. This document bears the Prosecution number 28, on the internal list, it's 61, and the PT number is 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding that the next document on the list has the internal number 58 and is actually another war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague is quite right. As far as the document that bears number 20 is concerned; that is to say, it's another excerpt from the 3rd Corps war diary. So we will move on to the document that has the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 58. That's the next document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's 51, according to your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was my mistake. The document number 20 has the internal number 58 and the PT number 60. This document, Mr. President, need not be examined yet again, because the arguments are the same as the ones that concern the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this war diary was on the list of the Defence to be discussed, and I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that this is not the very same war diary as we discussed earlier on today; it's a second war diary from the ABiH 3rd Corps covering the period of time May 1993 to July 1993. Since it was on the Defence list, I would please ask my learned friends from the Defence to raise their objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it's the same diary or not the diary, arguments are the same. We would like the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to provide the entire war diary and the translation so that we can be assured of the reliability of these documents and so that we can use these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this war diary is concerned that we will show to the accused, as opposed to war diary number 2, the colour of the diary is not the same; the cover is not the same either. The Trial Chamber notes that there is a number on the first page, number 3; in B/C/S it says, if I'm reading this correctly, "Ratni," and then there's the 16th of May, 1993. Below it it says, "Listova 1993".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1998, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in black felt-tip, we can see that something else has been written down at a subsequent date perhaps, but we can't be certain of that. So there are columns in this diary number 3 from 1 to 8. This isn't the case for the other diary. As in the case of diary number 2, there is -- there are handwritten parts with dates. The handwriting is different. As one of the parties said, it was the person on duty who took down notes. There are also pages written in black crayon, in black pencil. Show the document to the accused. Mr. Withopf, document 58, are you going to tell us -- are your arguments going to be the same for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: They will be very similar. It's an official document of the ABiH 3rd Corps; namely, a war diary, covering the period of time you just mentioned. Your Honour, Mr. President, it's relevant. The date of entry chosen by the Prosecution is the 9th of June, 1993 and shows the deployment of the OG Bosanska Krajina forces in Maljine, one of the killing sites that form part of the indictment. If the Trial Chamber wishes to request a full copy of the war diary and if the Trial Chamber wishes to have the full translation, the Prosecution would not object and would accommodate such a wish by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just one additional clarification: This diary, which contains eight columns, we can see that in column number 1 it mentions the time, and in column number 2 we have the minutes. In column number 1, we have the hours; and in column number the 2, we have the minutes. The details contained were taken down in real time, because in translation we can see that it says 2200 hours, 22.30.010, and the third -- the fourth reference is 0000. So there is something bizarre here. Why is there a "10" before "00"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the difference between the two documents - that is to say, the first one we had a look at a while ago - in our opinion the first diary was a war diary. This one here seems to be an operational diary. We're not certain about this, but it seems that this was a diary kept by an officer on duty or someone on duty in some command post within a certain unit. There are certain details from operational groups, and it concerns the situation in the operation group east and operation group west. It says the 308th Brigade, and as you said, Mr. President, the time is a bit confusing. And it mentions operational groups from Bosnian Krajina. Mr. President, our opinion is the reason for which this document shouldn't be admitted as it stands is that the Trial Chamber has to speculate about the document if it wants to use it, and these are concerns in relation to the reliability of the document. We do not have minimum probative value for this document in order to use it, if the document is not supported by other information. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document of the ABiH 3rd Corps -- of the ABiH 3rd Corps command in Zenica, and it has and is covering most relevant portions of the indictment. I can't understand why my learned friend is suggesting that such a document does not have the least minimum probative value to be admitted. It's the position of the Prosecution that the war diaries in particular have an extremely high probative value, since they stem from the very heart of the ABiH 3rd Corps command in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And as my colleague Mr. Mundis is emphasising, these are contemporaneous documents. They were written at the time, and there's hardly any better evidence to provide the Trial Chamber with that shows what happened at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that one of the accused can't hear again. THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] No, no, there was just something I wanted to say, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now have a break. I note that we have only examined five documents. We will have to move -- move on more rapidly, because we have only examined five documents. We will keep the pause to the minimum, and we will resume at five to 11.00. But before we adjourn, I would like to have another look at the war diary that the Defence called an operational diary. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, Mr. President, that my colleague says it's the operational diary from the 3rd Corps. That's what we wanted to say. The document you have in front of you, not the original but the piece of paper, we do not know whether it comes from the 3rd Corps or not. We need the entire diary in order to attach minimum probative value to it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll show the document -- I'll return the document to the Prosecution, and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume and try to speed things up. But first of all, I should like to inform the Defence and the Prosecution that the interpretation service has told us that the document which was in English with words in Arabic, the Arabic words would mean "in the name of God the merciful," and at the bottom, "There's only one God, Allah, and his prophet Muhammad." Those would be the religious words that we find on this document and not a signature, as we believed. If you wish, I can give a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would be most grateful, and the Prosecution is certainly very grateful to the court interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this is for your information. Mr. Withopf, I'm giving you -- This has to be shown to the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There's one brief issue, Your Honours. I had a brief talk with my learned friend, Mrs. Residovic, from the Hadzihasanovic Defence. In the second war diary, the light green one, there is actually an envelope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. There is actually an envelope contained, and the envelope contains a three-page document. For explanation, this envelope was found together with the war diary; therefore, it was kept together with the war diary, to make this absolutely clear. The envelope contains a three-page document from 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, I give you the floor, and let us move into second gear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I move on to the next document. It's a document with number 23 on the list; the internal number 61. Can I have the original, please. Regarding this document, it is a document which, if we look at the last page of the original document, is a document consisting of two lines for the signature with two signatures that we do not recognise. This document, Mr. President, for which the point of departure appears to be the headquarters of the army -- unfortunately, Mr. President, I don't have the English copy with me. It seems to have got lost during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can lend you ours. We can lend you ours, if you wish. You have it now, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, as you can see, on the original we have two signatures which we do not recognise. The document was sent from the Zenica Municipal Defence Staff, a unit that the Chamber has no information about so far. It was -- it is a report drawn up by the security and information office of the Zenica Municipal Defence Staff. This is an entity that is not a part of the 3rd Corps. It is separate from the headquarters of the 3rd Corps. And we see that the document appears to have been sent, one copy to the 3rd Corps organs and a copy to the Chief of Staff, or "staff commander" in the translation. But regarding evidence of sending and reception, we don't have any. There is a stamp making the document an official one, without doubt, but there are also several markings in hand. There are stars drawing attention to certain paragraphs and some passages were underlined, again, to draw attention to them. There is a note in handwriting which has been translated and which says that, "The security and information office, they have their copies." We believe, Mr. President, that in view of the shortcomings of this document, which doesn't give information about it being sent or received, cannot be admitted by the Chamber without additional support, the identity of the person who signed or approved it, who drafted the document, and what the purpose of the document was. As for the contents, we have no comment regarding the prima facie relevance, as well as the date. What we are saying is that the Chamber is faced with a document which has insufficient information to allow the Chamber to draw any conclusions from it unless they would be hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us show the -- have the document shown to the accused. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document is an authentic document obviously, as conceded by my learned friend. It's an official document, and it's from the Sarajevo collection 1. It's highly relevant. It's a Zenica Municipal Defence Staff report of 11 June 1993 related to the burning down of houses and looting in the area of Ovnak, and it makes reference that military personnel has to be regularly checked. The Municipal -- the Zenica Municipal Defence has been mentioned in paragraph 25 of the indictment; therefore, this is relevant. It's correct that there is no evidence whether it has been transmitted or not, at least not from the document. However, this again touches only on the probative value and not on the issue of the admissibility of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But wait a moment for us to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is, again, one of the war diaries, and I can make it available right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In document 61, or number 23, we see that it is a document that is typewritten. It has a stamp of the Municipal Staff of Zenica. We also note in the English translation in the first paragraph that the inspection of Ovnak required by the signatories, two of them, was carried out at the request of the staff commander. The staff commander, is that a military staff commander? That would be logical, particularly as the addressees are the 3rd Corps and the staff commander. So this could be an authority above the 3rd Corps. So that's as much as can be said at this stage. I am returning the document, and I'll give the floor to Mr. Bourgon for his next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I pass on to the next document, number 28 on the Prosecution list. It is a document that is an excerpt from a war diary. I have the original in my hands now. The same applies to this document. Judging by the original, two documents seem to have been extracted from this diary. The date is May 1993. And I also see an envelope in this document with a document inside, with a number, which consists of some sort of a list with a number. This number is not part of the document as such, though it has been given a number. Our arguments regarding this document, Mr. President, are that this is a document drafted by hand. We know from the translation of the document that there is a question regarding the date. If we look at the original document, we see that the date indicated is - I'm looking for the first page - it would be the 25th of June, at the bottom of the page; whereas, on the translation we have the date 23rd of June, 1993. If we look at the translation, there are several places, particularly page 2, a paragraph which mentions OGS Memisevic. There are several parts that are illegible. Also in the second -- in the following paragraph. So there are comments that have been added by the translator and several indications that passages are illegible. Now, if I try to find these passages in the original document -- I have the original here, and at the bottom of the page the name of a town is mentioned and the 25th of June, 1993; whereas, the translation says the 23rd of June. It could be a "3", I'm told. I'm looking at the handwritten entries, and our arguments regarding this diary is the same as for other documents from diaries. We would like the Chamber to ask the Prosecution to produce these diaries in totality with translations, which would meet the criterion of reliability. My learned friend from -- of the Kubura Defence may have some additional remarks to make regarding this document. We also note, Mr. President, that this appears to be a report on a meeting. What we don't know is to what extent the report reflects all -- everything that has been said or some of the things that were said and what is the state of that report. In our professional activities, be it as Defence or Prosecution, we have all attended meetings and witnessed minutes being made. The person making the minutes can go into great detail or can be very concise. And in a war context, this would be highly concise; hence the question of probative value. In any event, we need to have the whole diary to be able to judge the quality of information it contains. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will try to keep my answer very brief. Again, the Prosecution offers to tender a full copy of the full war diary. This stems from the Sarajevo collection, obviously. It's highly relevant. It's the date of 20 June, 1993. As my learned friend mentioned, it covers obviously the minutes of a meeting of the 3rd Corps commander, the accused Hadzihasanovic, with commanders of subordinated units, including the 7th Muslim Brigade commander at the time; namely, the accused Kubura. It's highly relevant in respect to command and control, to the deployment of units, and on page 4 it quotes a proposal made under 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and it says "Hiring foreign nationals." The technical issues that have been addressed by my learned friend have been addressed earlier on today. It's common that the interpreters make their comments in order to provide the ones who have to read the document with the information necessary. Such documents have in all proceedings before Trial Chambers in this Tribunal been accepted. That wasn't a major problem at all. The envelope which has been addressed at the beginning, this is exactly the envelope with a three-pages document which I had mentioned earlier on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will check once again the documents. So we note that they were written in blue pen. We also see that there's an envelope coming from the 3rd Corps with a document, a three-page document, inside which has not been translated, of course, and which is signed by the commander Brigadier Jusic with a stamp, "Commander, 3rd Corps," in blue. A moderately informed person could see that when there is an official document included in a diary of this kind, one can assume that it comes from the 3rd Corps. So I am returning the document to Mr. Withopf, and I'm asking Mr. Bourgon to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The next document is number 32. It is an order attributed to the accused General Hadzihasanovic because his block signature was used. It is a category of documents that we wish to draw the attention of the Chamber to. I have here the original document, which bears a signature which is unknown to us and which does not appear to be the signature of the accused. This order, Mr. President, with respect to transmission and reception, there's no mention of that on the original, except on the back of the document, and I see there that there is an indication in handwriting "325th Brigade, in Vitez." This is not to be found on the translation. No mention is made of the transmission in the English translation. We have a list of addressees on the second page of the document, and I'm talking about the translation. We have a list of the entities to which the document was addressed. However, there is no information as to the document having been sent. If we look at the original, Mr. President, one could conclude that this was a document produced mechanically with continuous pages, because we see there is a piece from another page attached, but a document of this kind with a handwritten signature, I think that the transmission would be found -- indicated in hand with a stamp. However, we have the number on the stamp; it is the Prosecution number 01821121. This number appears also on the back. We don't know whether the 325th Brigade of Vitez, which is mentioned on the back of the document, by whom this was added [as interpreted]. For these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that this is an order attributed to the accused, on the basis of his block signature. According to our arguments yesterday, a document of this kind cannot be tendered and used against the accused without having a witness who would come and tell us something about this document, its context, and its objective. Of course, the Chamber is capable of reading the document and making its own conclusions. And that is the gist of all our arguments. A document should not require any interpretation on the part of the Chamber, and the Chamber should be able to make its conclusions without asking itself any questions about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, when you talk of a block signature, how do you define this term? Does a block signature mean a stamp, name, and signature? How would you define the term "block signature"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A block signature, Mr. President, is what is found at the bottom of a document indicating the name and position of a person which, prima facie, appears to indicate that the document is attributed to that person. Our problem is that this document is attributed to the commander General Hadzihasanovic but the document is not signed by him. We don't know who signed it. We have no information as to who was authorised to sign on his behalf. More importantly - and we will see that in another document as well - normally in all administrations when a subordinate is authorised to sign on behalf of the superior, there is the word added "for." We will see some such documents later on. However, in this case, we have the block signature of the accused, but someone else has signed it. Was it used without the accused being aware of it, or did the accused authorise this person to sign? This may be put into evidence during the Defence case. But this document raises too many questions to be considered to be sufficiently reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of what you have said, the Chamber notes the following, before I give the floor to Mr. Withopf: Clearly this document has been faxed, because I see here too that the document at the top and at the bottom has an indication showing that this was a part of a series of documents, which you didn't mention. Also, there's a blue stamp. And as for the signature, there is a signature in green with a slash and then some words. In classical administrative law, everyone knows that when there is a slash, that means that whoever is signing is signing for someone. But we don't really know who actually signed. When one turns the document to the back, we see the "325th BBR Vitez." One can assume perhaps - but that is an assumption - that the said fax coming from the 3rd Corps -- but I also wish to say that there is an order number, 02/33-67. So it follows on to other previous orders. So it could be that this document was sent by the unit in Vitez, which is anyway mentioned among the addressees. "325th BBR," and we have here also "325th BBR Vitez." Maybe the archivist could tell us that indeed this document originated from the 325th Brigade. So those are the things we can note holding the document in our hands. I note also that there are holes on the left-hand side, which means that it was included in a binder. Are those holes made by the Prosecution? And I see that it -- that the holes coincide. Maybe it's the Prosecution that made those holes and not the archivist when the document was found. Though the photocopy that we have has other holes moved slightly to the right, which means that the photocopy that they gave us is a photocopy of the original which was part of a bigger document. You were able to note that the format of this document is not identical with the photocopy. Having made those notes and reservations, I return the document to Mr. Withopf, who will convey his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I may please very briefly first address the more technical issues Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, has just raised. The holes were not made by the Prosecution. The originals are in exactly the very same shape as they were found in the ABiH main archive. And Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, we already mentioned that this document in its original has a different format than the usual in A-4 format. Therefore, the copy shows on the right-hand side of the true holes, photocopied holes [sic]. If I may briefly address the other issues. This is, as I mentioned, a document from the Sarajevo collection 1. It's an official document of the ABiH. It's an order of the 3rd Corps. It's relevant. It's an order of the accused Hadzihasanovic. It shows command and control and subordination of troops. And the original itself shows that at the time - namely, in July 1993 - the 3rd Corps had at least quite sophisticated means to transmit such orders. The main issue, however, which has been addressed by my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence is the signature. Your Honour Mr. Presiding Judge has already made a number of remarks I would have made, so I don't need to repeat them. Since this issue, however, will be discussed probably in respect to a number of additional documents, it's correct. It's obviously or most likely, to be cautious, most likely not the signature of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. This is certainly not an unusual situation in the military. The commander of a corps - and we had witnesses who confirmed that the accused Hadzihasanovic was a commander who was quite often in the field - is not on a very regular basis always at his headquarters to sign any orders or any other documents. It's always - and it's pretty common in all militaries in the world - that there is a different person who is entitled to sign on behalf of the commander. The important issue, however, is that the order itself is still issued by the commander. Interpretation. There was a point addressed by my learned friend. This is a pretty straightforward order, and it doesn't require any particular knowledge. So in respect to the contents of the order, there's certainly not any room left for broader interpretations. This is the observations -- or these are the observations I wish to make at this stage in respect to this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are going to proceed. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm now addressing the next document, number 33. Could we have the original as well as the original of the previous document. Indeed, I would like to see this slash following the signature. I'd missed that before when I first looked at the document. Whilst I'm being given this document, let me underline regarding the last -- the previous document what our exact fears are. My colleague from the Prosecution said this is an order from the accused, so the Prosecution take for granted this is an order by the accused, while he has not signed the document. And that's the problem. That's where the problem lies, Mr. President. He says that it happens that way in all the armies in the world, but here we do not have the knowledge or the experience of all the armies in the world, and this is the proof or the evidence that we need in order to validate such a document. My colleague from the Prosecution is not able to provide us with such information. It must come from a staff, from an army; if not from that army, from an army functioning in the same way as to the signing of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll be able to put this question to the expert witness next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, I'm looking at it and I look only at the signature. I for one see the signature in a green ink, but I fail to see any slash that would show any kind, as you said in administrative law, of saying "for" or "on behalf." When such a mention is used, we'll see later on that it is stated quite clearly as such in the document. The next document, it bears the date of the 4th of July. I do have the original here in front of me. Once again, we're dealing with a document which is not signed. Well, it bears a signature, but it seems to be a different signature from the one we see in the block signature. And what I mean by that, it is the block signature of Mehmed Alagic as commander of the Operational Group Bosanska Krajina. So the document is sent by the operational group and is addressed to the motorised brigade, but we don't know which one it is, because it is illegible in the document. We do not know which brigade this document is sent to. We have a reception stamp, however, in the original, which I did not have, or which was illegible on the photocopy I was given, and which is not to be found in the original; whilst here it looks as if the document was received by the 312th Brigade, which is something I couldn't find. I did not have on the document I used to work. So this is one less shortcoming as to this document. Mr. President, the Trial Chamber will recall that this was a document presented by the Prosecution when we had a witness, witness Eminovic last week. This witness was not able to recognise the said order, and since he failed to recognise it, it was not tendered into evidence. As it was not tendered into evidence, today the Prosecution is asking us to accept the document whilst, although, this document that the witness whose name is mentioned was not able to recognise the document. If a name is mentioned, if a witness is unable to recognise the document, it casts serious doubt as to the very existence or the drafting or the sending of the order. This is an additional factor added to the technical shortcomings. As a result, such a document cannot be used by the Trial Chamber without further information, without further evidence being adduced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber apprises the document, which is very useful. It's useful to see it because we can see that this document is of the same origins as the previous ones, inasmuch as it was sent electronically, so it was sent by fax or with a system of continuous pages. As to the -- this is just an observation. The quality of the paper is the same as that of the paper we've seen before. There are two holes that are punched here as well. There is a stamp, a very official stamp of the 312th Brigade, so the brigade must have received the document and stamped it. However, there is something else that was not mentioned so far by the Defence: This document apparently comes from Mr. Alagic. It is an answer to another document which number 03/1001774 from the 3rd Corps, [In English] "in reply to." [Interpretation] In other words, it is the logical sequence of a previous document. Very well. So these are the observations made by the Trial Chamber without taking a stance as to the substance of the document, so just looking at it, the colours, the punched holes. As to the signatures, rightly so the Defence argued that in the block signature there was no signature, that there was one signature at the bottom. But if this document is a document that came by telex or by other means of receiving, there's no signature. However, we can see a signature at the bottom; it may be the signature of the person who received the document and who authenticates the reception of the document. So these are technical observations. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, very briefly. Again, it appears that this document was sent and that it for that reason doesn't contain a signature above the signature block, a pretty common and usual situation. If I may please address the one issue that this document, what's completely correct, has been shown to the witness Jasenko Eminovic last week. The Prosecution, however, does not only put weight on this document in respect to the function the witness Jasenko Eminovic had at the time. The relevance goes far beyond it. It says, and it makes reference to an ABiH military person in Mehurici. This document is dated the 4th of July, 1993, and order a march of prisoners to Zenica under the 306 command. Obviously a highly relevant document. So the issue that the witness Eminovic was not in a position to recognise this document shouldn't play a role. I wish, however, to add that the Prosecution has not withdrawn the document; the document has been marked for identification and it's P104 ID. Again, the Prosecution is of the view this may be discussed under whatever aspects of the probative value. However, the reasons put forward by my learned colleague doesn't diminish the probative value to the extent that it cannot be considered being an admissible document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Bourgon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I move on to the next document in the list, document number 43. Mr. President, this is a document lacking, once again, a signature. It originates from the west or Zapad Operational Group and addressed personally to the commander of the 3rd Corps; namely, the accused General Enver Hadzihasanovic. So this is a very important and relevant document with regard to the information that would be available to the accused. Looking at the document that we have here, there is no evidence of it being sent or received. I observe that at the back of the document there's a sign that mentions indeed continuous paper, so it may have been that there were other documents before and after this one. You can find the letters "L" and "AC", but it might be that it was the printer that would print out continuously, one document after the other. There are illegible parts in the document, so we should ask ourselves whether the accused did indeed receive the document or whether it was sent. A moment ago we had a document, judging by the observations that we could make had been sent and it did bear an original signature. In this instance, there is no signature. One individual is identified in the document, but there is no original signature. There is a mention at the top of the document that mentions the time, which is 10.15. There are numbers in red ink, and these are the numbers written in by the Prosecution. There is a handwritten mention at the top of the document as well. Mr. President, if this goes to the acts and behaviour of the accused - because here we're talking about the knowledge he might have had - then you have to prove that the document was received by the accused. Do we believe regarding admissibility that such a document without further evidence, without even knowing whether it was sent or received, is it sufficient? We do not think so, in terms of admissibility. We merely want to have some kind of evidence. In this document, you have a number or numbering, and we don't know -- we do not know how documents were numbered. We do not know whether they would follow each other or whether there was the same system across to the operational group, say, and the 3rd Corps. So we do not know -- we do not think that such a document is reliable without further evidence; otherwise, it is just too many questions that you have to ask ourselves. You don't know whether it was sent or received or even it was drafted by the individual mentioned at the bottom of the document. A last comment: With regard to the translations of documents. Often we find a mention - and this is page 2, last line of the document - we see a heading that says "Sent to," or forwarded to [In English] "Commander, 3rd Corps" [Interpretation] And then file. And under the heading you have [In English] "stamp and signature." [Interpretation] So this is the translation that mentions that. But if I look at the original, I find the same mention, but it doesn't mean that there is a stamp. It merely shows or indicates that this document was meant to receive a stamp, but the stamp is not there. The other document with the same quality of paper that had been sent by this machine had a signature and a stamp; not the case here. On the contrary. And we do not refer to the substance of the document. The substance seems quite relevant, and that applies to the date as well, which is September.
