But we doubt whether we can rely on the document as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to look at the document, after the accused have seen it. Did you want to add anything, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Just an additional piece of information. The document you have in your hands has a page that was prepared by the investigators of the OTP. It's some kind of an analysis. The analysis part should not be confusing as to the quality of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not looking at the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure about it. That's not the point. The point is, of course, that the Prosecution had unbelievable means at its disposal to carry out this type of analysis, which is not the case for the Defence. But the analysis is not part and parcel of the document. That's the only thing we wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this document, looking at it, we can see that this document is part of a sequence of documents. There again, you can see it is indented at the top and at the bottom, so we can see that it is part of a sequence of documents. We also observe something which was not said: At the back of the document we can see "TSDAC." It must be the brand of paper, judging by it, because there is a follow-up to that. So it must be the -- actually the trademark of the paper. Obviously it would be very easy for the Prosecution to identify the origin of the paper. And there are two holes, as usual, and indeed there is no signature. You have the name of the commander of the Zapad Operational Group, Mr. Selmo Cikotic. However - and this was not stated by the Defence - under the text you find this "SEC/NA." "SEC," the acronym is probably -- well, the initials of the commander, Selmo Cikotic; and "NA" it must be his or her secretary or the person in charge of drafting or typing the document. This is a tradition in all the administrations of the world. The initials of the author of the document are in the document as well as the initials of the typist. This may have escaped Mr. Bourgon, but it is stated; you have the slash with "NA." So this is the format of this document. The paper may look similar, in terms of quality, to the other documents we've seen previously. Mr. Withopf, and I am going to return the document to you without looking at the comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This document, as has been mentioned by my learned friend, is highly relevant. It's highly relevant to notice and knowledge of the accused Hadzihasanovic in respect to the detention facilities in Bugojno. This is one of the documents - and the Prosecution is very happy to have been enabled by the Defence to discuss this particular document - this is one of the documents -- documents which shows what we said yesterday; this is a circumstantial case, and documents must not be looked in an isolated manner at. I yesterday mentioned there are sometimes a series of documents and the full evidence is only -- can only be seen once one had a look at a second document. The next document which will be discussed and which is on the list of the Defence is exactly the answer of the accused Hadzihasanovic to this document. And, Your Honours, Mr. President, you will see once you have the next document in your hands that this is making reference to the document you had in front of you a few seconds ago. This situation very strongly -- very strongly supports the argument made yesterday by the Prosecution that it is not possible to only look at one document to judge on the issue of admissibility. Documents - and that applies to all documents - must be seen together with other evidence, with other documents, and must be seen together with any other evidence such as witness testimony before this Court. Therefore, I'm actually very happy to have been -- had the opportunity -- to have had the opportunity to discuss this document, and I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the next document, which confirms that the first document has been sent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bourgon, I suppose you're going to move on to the next document, which is the reply to the previous document. So basically we have two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, the following document bears number -- the number 44. This is a document addressed to the commander of the Bosanska Krajina Operational Group. I'm not sure that I've got the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't have it, we can lend you ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. I now have the original in my hands. There is a signature. We can see the signature block of the accused, so this document is attributed to the commander of the 3rd Corps. However, the signature in the document is not the commander's -- the 3rd Corps commander's signature. Now, I'm looking at the back of the document, and I can see that there is evidence that it was sent, but that sort of receipt was not enclosed -- oh, yes, it is. It was enclosed through the translation of the document. We therefore can see that allegedly this document was sent at 20 hours 26 minutes on the 19th of September. There are other numbers that are indicated, except that we do not have any information regarding such numbers. Beforehand we had a document personally addressed to the commander of the 3rd Corps, an unsigned document. Here we have a reply which is attributed to the commander and bears the signature of another individual and doesn't either have the "for" mentioned; that is, on behalf of the accused. So we do not know whether the document, in spite of the number, the stamp at the back, we do not know whether the document can be attributed to the accused without the presence of any further evidence, which is the system that was applied within the 3rd Corps. We quite agree as to the relevance of this document. There's no problem about the dates. The question is the following: We have two documents that follow each other. We're not playing any games. We could have separated those two documents. We want to see them together. No, we argue that for the Trial Chamber to be able to use a document that is tendered into evidence without a witness, without additional evidence, it is worse because it is attributed to the accused in person, and we know that the signature is not the accused's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Usher, please give us the document, first to the Judges and then to the accused. We just want to check something. I'm going to pass the document on to the accused, and then it will be returned to the Prosecutor. What is the observation? As usual, we have punched holes. The quality of the paper, well, it is a paper that comes from a recording system. The best evidence of it is that you can see sort of stripes at the back of the document. This is a first regarding these documents. There is the stamp of the 3rd Corps with the receipt date, a number, 2080, a date is also mentioned, it is the date of the 19th of September, 1993, 20 hours and 26 minutes. On the other hand, regarding the issue of the signature, we observe that there is a stamp in blue ink, which means that the blue stamp is not the stamp at the time when the document is sent, because you do not send coloured documents, documents in colour. In other words, the stamp that you can see is the one that was put onto the document when it was received. As for the signature to be found here, it must have been the signature of the individual that received the document, which accounts for the fact that it is not the signature of the author of the document. So forensically speaking, this is what can be said as to this document, judging by the look of it. You have the signature, the stamp -- various stamps. Now, the issue of the relevance is something else, but we observe that the contents of the reply is a reply to the first document, because I can see in the first paragraph what is said. It is said that it agrees to liaison officers being appointed, and that was the question that had been mentioned in the previous document. Very well. Madam Usher, please give the document to the accused, and Mr. Withopf you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I do not want to repeat myself. This is again the issue of the signature. The Prosecution has made its observations on a number of occasions today. It may or may not be an issue of the probative value, but certainly not an issue of the admissibility of the documents. I, however, wish to very briefly draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that left to the signature you have the official -- the very official stamp of the ABiH 3rd Corps, what shows that this is a very official document. This - and I do not want to speculate - but I have seen signatures of the deputy commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps, Mr. Dzemal Merdan, and at a first glance it may appear to me that this signature -- this "M" is actually Mr. Merdan's signature. However, I do not want to speculate at this junction about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The next document bears the number 45. This document is part of a different category, as it is a document which does carry the signature block of the accused but with the specific mention "for" the accused. This brings me to a remark that was said in connection with the previous document, as there are some similarities. As I don't have the original with me, I don't know the colour, but I'll be able to do -- see that in a minute. I'm looking at the document now, and I do see a blue stamp and a signature, which could be, according to the judgement of the Chamber, the assumption of the Chamber, which is quite reasonable, that this could have been stamped upon reception and signed by the person receiving it. Nevertheless, my friend from the Prosecution underlined something very interesting, that this was the stamp of the 3rd Corps. It can hardly be put upon the reception of the document as the document emanated from the 3rd Corps and was sent to another place. My learned friend also appears to recognise the initials of the signatory, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. Could he have been in the Zapad Operational Group and that is why he signed it, or was he with the 3rd Corps? All these hypotheses go in support of the Defence thesis that the document as such is not reliable. It is certainly that it is important to see these documents that affect the substance and have probative value, but can we attribute this document to the accused when we don't have sufficient information? The signature that we do have in our hand just now, if we look at the signature block we see initials. I didn't mention it before. You noted very well a moment ago there was something signed by Selmo Mikotic [as interpreted] with the initials "SM." I didn't notice it. Now I see "HH/TA." So I don't know who is HH, who drafted the document, nor who was the person who typed the document. I do know, however, that someone, whose signature I don't recognise, did sign it for the commander. Did the commander give instructions to someone to sign a document on his behalf? We know that in public administrations when a superior officer authorises a subordinate to sign a document on his behalf, there are explicit instructions to that effect, and surely this can be found in the archives. The Prosecution had access to those archives and we don't have that information. In the case of the document we have in front of us addressed to the commander of the Bosanska Krajina Group, a document which mentions the sender - I have the original - it also has punched holes, and it would appear that the 3rd Corps sent it at 11.30 on the 18th, I think - I can't see exactly - probably the 18th of October, 1993. October 1993. And the person who signed it is someone we do not know. He signed it in a specific manner, specifically for the commander. One might ask oneself what one should do with a document that is not signed, one that is signed by someone else, by another one signed for the commander. All these points, from the technical point of view, raises the question as to whether one can use the document without additional evidence. That is the only point we are making, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the document and we'll show it to the accused. Again, it is the same type of paper that we've already seen. It fits within a series of documents that must have come through a machine, because there are traces here that it has been cut. There are punched holes, as has been indicated. As the Defence tells us, on the back there is a stamp registering the document on the 18th of October, 1993, and mention is made of the 3rd Corps, and a signature appears. There's also a stamp of the 3rd Corps in blue, again with a signature. This document has an indication "Urgent" - probably in B/C/S it's also "Urgent," the same word - then there's a number also, "02/332273." So the following one would be 2274 and the previous one 2272, and the 22 -- it's 2273. It could be 22 hours 13, but it's probably not 22.13 but 22.73 as a number. So that is the appearance of this document. And one can also see along the length of the paper a black trace which comes from the machine -- the receiving machine, which seems to be faulty because the ink is causing problems and it's quite visible the whole length of the piece of paper. Let us show the document to the accused. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What I, Mr. President, again wish to emphasise in this context: This is a very official document of the ABiH 3rd Corps command. It's the request of the accused Hadzihasanovic for submission of information in respect to the massacre in Maljine, and it stems from the Sarajevo collection 1. It's obviously highly relevant to the massacre in Maljine. It shows notice and knowledge of the accused Hadzihasanovic in that respect. And I refer to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief for further details. The issue has been again addressed about the signatures. I do not, in order to not waste time, to in a stereotype manner to always repeat myself. The true issue is we have an official document that stems from an official archive that has official stamps on it. It's obvious it's an official document. I gave some, in my view, reasonable explanations in respect to many of the issues related to the signatures. And the only issue we are talking about is the following: Does the fact that somebody else signed a document, instead of the person who is mentioned on the -- what's called the signature block, or does the fact that there is no signature, or does the fact there is only an initial, does this render the probative value or does it diminish the probative value of such a document, such a highly official document, does it make the probative value so little that it cannot be admitted? And it's the Prosecution point of view that none of the official documents face such a situation. They are official documents, and it's an issue of probative value but not -- certainly not an issue of the admissibility of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, please. We have a quarter of an hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the next document bears the number 116. It is a report attributed to the -- I'm sorry. According to the Prosecution list, it is number 50 on the Prosecution list. It's a document dated the 8th of November, 1993. This document, Mr. President, in reference to the debate that we had yesterday and the submissions we made regarding the ratione temporis of the indictment, this document was drafted on the 8th of November, 1993 by the new commander - at least prima facie - so this document could be attributed to the new commander of the 3rd Corps; that is, Mr. Mehmed Alagic. And if we look at the document, on the signature page - I have the original in front of me, which I'm going to look at - there is a signature with a stamp of the 3rd Corps, but we do not recognise the signature on this document. Is it the signature of the commander of the 3rd Corps, or is it the signature of somebody who signed on his behalf? The letters to the left, we find "AS" and "MS"." Does this apply to the drafting of the document or the typing of the document? Those letters do not correspond to "MA," as Mehmed Alagic. So we don't know whether Commander Alagic drafted the document, signed the document, or gave instructions for the production of that document. However, looking at the back of the document, there's an indication that says that this document appears to have been sent on the 8th of November, and again there's a signature that we don't recognise. If we look at the contents of this document, without entering into a detailed analysis we can see that the document as such is not relative to the acts of General Hadzihasanovic. My colleague from the Kubura Defence might comment on it as well because it is dated the 8th of November, 1993. This is a document, Mr. President, when our client was no longer commander of the 3rd Corps. This document, according to the submissions we made yesterday, to be used against him needs to have additional guarantees regarding reliability, because we come across the same problems with respect to the signature, the handwritten notes, and also we don't know who gave instructions for such a document to be drafted on the 8th of November, 1993. Those would be our observations, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will examine the document. Here again it is the same type of order, sent by -- through a transmission system. The documents could be cut, and we see evidence of that. There are several holes in it, which means that it must have been folded to be cut in half because it wasn't cut in the middle. It could have been cut in half, but it is rather long, and that's why it was folded. This document to the left has two dates in the B/C/S language. There's the 8th of November, 1993, and above that, the 13th of November, 1993. On the back, there is a stamp in blue and also a stamp of the 3rd Corps with the arrival date 13th of November, 11 hours 45 minutes. So regarding the signature, we have the same problem again; there is a stamp in colour, which may be the arrival stamp. There is some scribbling, and before that, there is a line. Does this mean that the person who receives it stamps it and signed it, or is it the person who sent the document? We don't know that. Regarding relevance, there is a paragraph, we are told, relative to the 7th Corps which was placed at the disposal of the 7th Corps, and according to the command they felt it was necessary to integrate them within the 3rd Corps. I'm referring to the last paragraph of the English translation. In this document translated into English, the stamp "ECV" means electronic communications centre. That is in B/C/S. And in English it must be the same translation. Maybe the system of communication was of an American or British origin, and that is why this abbreviation is used. We are going to give the document to the accused. And, Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, very briefly, taking into account that we are close to the next break and so far we have only discussed 12 out of the 46 or 50 documents which we were supposed to discuss today. I'm a bit surprised that my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence has selected this document, since it's obviously not related to the accused Hadzihasanovic. As Your Honour Mr. Presiding Judge already stated, this document deals with the involvement of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in Vares and it makes reference to the cases -- cases of looting of members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in Vares. I refer to paragraph 45 of the Third Amended Indictment. In respect to the signatures, I do not need to repeat myself. I wish to emphasise, however, that the very same statement applies to this document as to many other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 25 past 12.00. We will have a break. We will resume at ten to 1.00. In view of the delay, which is understandable, in view of the technical discussions, if we don't finish today, we will continue at a later stage, obviously not next week, because we have a witness planned. We will have to find a date to continue the examination of these documents. There's no other way. Let us adjourn, and we will resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. Mr. Withopf, there was something you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the Prosecution, I wish to make a suggestion. As mentioned earlier on today, so far we have discussed 12 or so out of the 50 documents to be discussed. With the current pace, that would mean we would need at least two to three additional full court days to discuss the remaining 30 or so documents. The Prosecution is not really sure whether this is really necessary, and we are not sure whether this is necessary for the following reason: Defence has indicated that they wish to discuss documents and alleged difficulties and problems with such documents by way of example. We had a number of examples, and as it became obvious over the last 30 to 45 minutes prior to the break, many of such examples concern the issue of signatures, and I repeatedly mentioned that I do not want to repeat myself, since the Prosecution's point of view has been made very clear in this respect on numerous occasions, as has the Defence point of view on the very same issues. So I'm not really sure whether the very same issues have to be discussed in respect to another 30 or 35 of such documents. It's the Prosecution's view that these documents are admissible. The only issue - and it was quite interesting to see that today the key word was "probative value," quite often even in the submission of the Defence - the probative value is a different thing, but the admissibility, I think, it became quite clear that due to the fact the documents are official, very official documents, there's no reason why they shouldn't be admitted. And the Prosecution is again making reference to the manner how the Kvocka Trial Chamber approached this very same issue. I, for the Prosecution, suggest that we may discuss a few more such documents, but I don't see the need to discuss all 50 of them. Of course, I see the point that the Kubura Defence wishes to address a number of documents. It would be also beneficial for the Prosecution to know better sooner than later what the decision of the Trial Chamber would be in respect to the admission of documents for a reason that has already been addressed yesterday: The Prosecution, as mentioned yesterday, will continue to discuss documents with witnesses to come; however, the number of documents to be discussed with such witnesses will certainly depend on the Trial Chamber's decision on the admission of the documents, of all the documents which are currently on the exhibit list. I do not want to mention any practical issues involved, such as the fact that the documents have to be signed in, to be signed out, to be signed in and to be signed out again and again and again, what may touch upon the quality of the originals of the documents. To summarise this, the Prosecution doesn't see the need to continue for additional two to three court days to discuss the very same issues, and it became apparent that we reached a point in time where we're just repeating -- Defence is repeating their point of view, we are repeating our point of view; the positions of the two parties are pretty clear. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to the Defence to comment on your position. The Prosecution has said that given what has been said up until now and on the basis of all the documents that we have examined, the Defence is now in a position to present in a concise manner its case without examining the other documents. And we could then give the floor to Mr. Dixon to comment on the documents that concern Mr. Kubura. This is an approach that we could follow. The Chamber has noted the interest of examining the original documents, which are very telling, and this could have enabled the Defence that perhaps had certain misconceptions with regard to certain problems -- this may have permitted the Defence to get a better view, have a clearer idea of the documents. I'm referring to the operational diaries, the war diaries, or the orders that were forwarded via the electronic system in force at the time, or by telex in particular, because I personally think that most of the orders that we have were forwarded by telex. Mr. Bourgon, as far as the Prosecution's idea is concerned, to move on more rapidly, what would you say? We have about one more hour. What is your position? And then I will let Mr. Dixon take the floor. Because examining documents has enabled us to clear up certain ambiguities as far as the signatures, stamps, et cetera, are concerned. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As is the case for the Prosecution, the Defence would also like to move on more rapidly in order to save time. Nevertheless, Mr. President, this procedure, wanting to have 650 documents admitted into evidence by simply saying that these documents are relevant, the Chamber won't be in a position to assess the probative value. This causes certain problems, Mr. President: When we arrive at the end of this case, no one doubts that there will be about 50 or 100 documents that will be important and relevant and which will really have something to contribute to the outcome of the case in one way or another, but the Prosecution adopts the shotgun approach. One fires at random and we're sure to hit something, but they do this without providing any support for the other documents and leave it to the Trial Chamber to attach weight to these documents, and then they would plead, make submissions, and try to establish links between the documents. Yesterday the Trial Chamber presented the notion of a fair trial. Mr. President, for a fair trial, it's necessary for the Defence to have documents at their disposal. That is in fact the case. Defence also requires sufficient time to examine and to analyse the documents. We have had sufficient time to do so, in particular with regard to the Sarajevo collection. We have had these documents for some time now, for over two years. The issue that you raised yesterday, which concerned a fair trial, concerned the opportunity of contesting a document, contesting charges within the framework of an adversarial debate. The Defence's position, Mr. President, is that these documents, the 650 documents, not to mention all the other documents that we have already admitted into evidence - and we have serious reservations about them - but we agreed to have them admitted in order to facilitate the proceedings and so as not to obstruct the proceedings. In our opinion, Mr. President, these documents, when they are not reliable, this has an effect on the relevance and it can't be used for the Prosecution's case. So this is an integral part of the need for a fair trial. Because once documents have been admitted into evidence, they constitute proof, and then anything can happen. It is the duty of the Defence when presenting its case to address each document that has been admitted into evidence because, Mr. President, we do not know what is happening on the other side of the line that we call admissibility. The Trial Chamber will rule, it will assess the documents, and we respect this. But once the documents have gone over to the other side, have crossed the line, then it is our duty to contest these documents officially. We want to save time. We don't want to waste the Trial Chamber's time. But at the same time, there are certain other documents that we would like to deal with. I think I could discuss five or six additional documents, no more, and then we will have used these examples to illustrate our case to the Trial Chamber. But I think it is important to do so, Mr. President, because in our opinion the technical difficulties raised are only examples. We believe that afterwards the Trial Chamber should examine each document. The Trial Chamber won't have the originals at that stage, so all the conclusions that we are reaching today, as far as the colours, blue, green, and red are concerned, and the notes contained in the documents, these should be applied to the other documents, because unless the Trial Chamber asks for the originals, it will be very difficult for the Trial Chamber to rule. With your permission, Mr. President, I'll move on to the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. So you said you would have about five documents. Mr. Dixon, in view of what the Prosecution has said, how many documents would you like to deal with? Because I am keeping an eye on the time. I'm listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I said yesterday, Your Honours, we have divided the documents that we contest into a number of categories, and we have prepared under each heading a list of all of the documents, the main documents that affect Mr. Kubura, and that list is available. I can make it available at the end of the hearing today. There are nine categories altogether, with the different documents listed underneath, which fit under each category. All I wish to do, Your Honours, is to use an example from each of those categories, so approximately nine to ten documents. I don't require the originals in the case of every document either; only in the case of a few that are allegedly signed by Mr. Kubura. And I have worked out I could do that in about 45 minutes. I would support Mr. Bourgon's submission that he be allowed to continue with a further selection of his documents and perhaps thereafter - it might not be today - but for about 45 minutes to an hour at the beginning of another hearing I could go through these categories. Your Honours did initially set aside, I think, four to five days for this hearing, and we've only had three. So if it was to run over today, I wouldn't need much more time. Perhaps on Monday before General Reinhardt or -- or perhaps before another witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will withdraw to deliberate. We'll try to do so quickly. Unfortunately, as the President of the Trial Chamber, I can't control all these practical issues. I would have dealt with them very rapidly. But I have to consult the Judges. Therefore, we will withdraw and we'll be back in a few minutes' time. --- Break taken at 1.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. The Trial Chamber has deliberated, and the ruling is composed of two elements: First of all, there's an oral decision. We are requesting that the Prosecution provide us with all the originals of all the documents included on the Prosecution's list. We would like to be provided with all the originals. As far as practical issues are concerned, the Prosecution will deal with this issue with the Chamber's legal officer, but the Trial Chamber must be in a position to rule by examining the originals, because this morning we have noted how important the originals are when compared to the copies of these documents. So this is the first part of our decision. The second part of our decision concerns the following: We will allow Mr. Bourgon to illustrate his arguments with the five or six documents he mentioned, and then we will let Mr. Dixon discuss the nine or ten documents he has to discuss. If we do not manage to deal with all these documents, we will continue to discuss the matter on another day, because it is absolutely necessary to engage in an adversarial debate with regard to these essential issues. Mr. Bourgon, without wasting any more time, you may proceed to comment on these five or six documents. Yes, Mr. Withopf, there's something you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's a pure technical matter. The Prosecution would be very grateful if Defence counsel, in particular the Defence for Mr. Kubura, could identify which documents they wish to have discussed in particular. And the second technical issue is in respect to the originals. When does the Trial Chamber expect to be provided with the originals? To sign out about 600 documents from the Evidence Unit takes an incredible amount of time, since 600 accompanying forms have to be filled in to some detail. So it would be very beneficial for the Prosecution to get to know as to when the Trial Chamber expects this procedure be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to the timing, it would be best to do this as soon as possible, naturally. As far as the forms are concerned, you showed us a while ago -- Madam Usher, could you obtain an example of one of the documents we have already examined from the Prosecution with these forms, with these examples of signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the forms, the record of the exhibits, we can see that there is the name, the date of the person it was sent to. We can see the reason, the person who received the document, and we can see a date. As each document has such a form, it's necessary -- it's sufficient for the legal officer of the Chamber to sign and date the document or the registrar to do so, and then the document can be given to the Chamber by the Prosecution. This is not an obstacle that can't be overcome, because you are the custodian of these documents, but given that the Trial Chamber is requesting these documents so that they can be examined, the Trial Chamber would as a result take over the custody of these documents. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This is exactly the point, Mr. President, I was trying to make. In practical terms, and to -- in order to accelerate proceedings, may I please suggest that the Trial Chamber's legal officer gets in direct contact with the Evidence Unit; otherwise, the whole procedure would have to be done twice, what would make things obviously more complicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right. And that would enable us to move on rapidly and to avoid problems with regard to taking over custody of the documents in question. It would also be good if on the basis of these categories Mr. Dixon could inform us of the documents that he wanted to refer to by basing himself on these categories. This would enable the Prosecution to respond to his arguments. But you have time to think about that. You will take the floor a little later. Mr. Bourgon, with regard to the five or six documents you want to discuss, you may proceed. You will inform us of the number; the usher will fetch the document. We will proceed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to discuss document number 69, and in order to do so I need the original. The only issue that we want to raise, and it's a new issue in relation to the other documents, is the fact that the document is illegible -- a significant part of the document is illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite correct. The copy that we have is illegible. We'll examine the original to see whether it is also illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am looking at the original, and it's the same as the photocopy; that is to say, there are at least three paragraphs that are illegible. Although, it might be possible if we use the original to read it. But I note that the translation service wasn't able to read the document, to read this part. Our comments are the same, as far as the signature and other details are concerned, that the illegible nature of the document is what is specific to this document. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will examine the document. Thank you. In fact, we note that the first and second paragraph it's been typed. These are typewritten paragraphs. And the typewriter's ribbon must have been deficient. So if we look at the document, if we look through the document, you can see that it was typewritten. Theoretically we might be able to reconstitute the text. If a little effort were made, we could reproduce what the text actually says. As far as the relevance is concerned, given that the Prosecution has produced this document, it's primarily paragraphs 3, 4, and the others that are of interest, and the first two paragraphs are not of great interest to the Prosecution. That would be the conclusion. Mr. Withopf, what do you have to say about this document? We will then move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, you already with your comment have pre-empted what I wanted to say. It's obviously the Prosecution's point of view that the portions which are legible are the relevant ones. The document in its legible portions shows that it is an official document. Therefore, the Prosecution doesn't consider the fact that portions which are or may or may not be relevant are not legible. Again, I don't think this is an issue for admissibility; again, more for probative value. If one has a close look at the document, it appears to me that it actually is legible. But I'm certainly not going to debate this issue in greater detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will show this document to the accused. There is just something I would like to point out: This document has a stamp from the 3rd Corps, and below it says "Operational Group Krajina," which shows that the group was part of the 3rd Corps and that there were specific stamps for certain units. This is something that we haven't seen yet. And thanks to the original, we can see that such cases existed. That is why it's important and interesting to see the original documents. Madam Usher, could you show the accused this document. Mr. Bourgon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while the accused are examining the document, in our opinion it's not the assessment of the Prosecution about the relevance of the document; it's the Trial Chamber's assessment of the document that is important. I'll move on to the document -- to document number 71. Mr. President, it's not necessary for me to examine the original document, since the additional remark that I have to make with regard to this document concerns the type of document. This is an authorisation given by Commander Alagic -- that was apparently given by Commander Alagic and was allegedly given to a person called Rasim Razic [phoen], who was accompanied by a driver. Perhaps it concerned a laissez-passez, or perhaps it was a matter of granting authorisation to pass between two towns. This was a period for when the laissez-passez was valid. Mr. President, we do not know who the individual in question is. We still have the same problem with regard to the signature. We do not know if the individual received this document or if the document was sent. Likewise, we do not know if use was made of this document, and we have no information about the Travnik firefighting unit. Likewise, we have no information on the civil defence headquarters in Travnik. The document on its own, without any additional supporting material, cannot be used in a useful way by the Trial Chamber unless the Trial Chamber speculates, and for this reason we do not think that the Trial Chamber should admit this into evidence without any supporting material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there is another problem in that the Trial Chamber does not have an English translation of the document at its disposal; all we have is the B/C/S version. Mr. Withopf, you have heard the Defence's arguments concerning the fact that this document relates to an individual whose identity is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's correct, there is no English translation in the binder. I'm obviously confronted with the same problem as Your Honours. I, however, still wish to hand over the original, since the Trial Chamber requested to get all of the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There are two punched holes on the original, as indicated. It was typewritten. It can be seen when you look at the document or through the document. There is a stamp from the 3rd Corps with the "BK" Bosanska Krajina Operational Group. And there is a signature under the name of "Alagic." But before the word "commander," there's also something. There is a number and a date, the date of the 12th of June, 1993. So this is the document as it can be observed by us without any further comment. Madam Usher, please present this document, the original, to the Defence and the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, nothing further to add regarding this document. Can this document be used as such without speculating? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this document, Mr. Withopf, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We will certainly provide the Trial Chamber on short notice with a translation of this document. It's obviously a very brief document, so this issue can be dealt with within a reasonable time frame. Otherwise, it's again the issue of signatures, which has been discussed repeatedly. And I'm making reference to what I said earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The next document bears the number 90, whilst the original is being given to me, let me go back quickly on something. Just an observation regarding document 79, the one that was illegible. My colleagues tell me of course with a caveat that the three -- the first three paragraphs relate to civil protection and also relate to the prohibition of looting. So it looks as if the first three paragraphs are indeed very relevant. And there are many documents of this type that are illegible among the documents proposed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you say that this deals with relevant issue, that means that you were able to read illegible documents. So you have an incredible extraordinary faculty, that of reading documents characterised as illegible. You can go two ways: Either the Prosecution will complete the translation of documents, or the Defence will provide the contents of the allegedly illegible documents that you were, however -- paragraphs that you were, however, able to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same question, Mr. President: If the documents remain as such, the Chamber cannot use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 90. It is a diary -- it is a newspaper bearing the title "Patriotski List." It is a newspaper bearing the date of the 30th of November, 1993. It is a publication in which you can find an interview with General Hadzihasanovic, and as reported by this document, the interview is with the general and he speaks about the formation of the army -- or more specifically, of the 3rd Corps. Mr. President, in the Defence view, such a newspaper -- well, we all know what worth or value to give to media productions. They can be true or just absolutely untrue. And we argue that all these journals, newspapers, and articles, even if the substance is relevant, must be appreciated through a witness. We must know to what extent or in which way the words were taken by the journalist so as to attach enough reliability so that you can say, "Yes, this is indeed an interview with the accused and we know in which circumstances it took place." Regarding such a document, you really need to have a witness who is going to come and explain in which way and when he met the accused. So this is in a direct connection with the acts and conduct of the accused. And as we said yesterday in our arguments, when the acts and conduct of the accused are involved directly, since here it is him talking, it is basically sort of lending faith to a statement without knowing whether it is a statement and whether its content is true and accurate. So we need a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the original, do we? What do you say, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I may draw your attention to page 1 of this magazine. At the top right-hand corner, there's the official stamp of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is an official magazine of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This, Mr. President, Your Honours, is a very typical example of the issue of probative value. Of course the Prosecution shares the view of Defence counsel that a media report can be attached the same high probative value as to a witness testimony or any other document. However, there still is a probative value. In particular, in this situation, when the statements made by the accused Hadzihasanovic in the course of this interview are bolstered by other evidence - and the Prosecution would be in a position to do so - this is exactly the document which has been discussed already yesterday. Defence in their 19th of April submission challenged this document amongst other things, because document is external to ABiH 3rd Corps HQ. But I still don't understand if the commander of the 3rd Corps gives an interview, I don't see how this can be external. The accused Hadzihasanovic has provided quite a bit of detailed information about the establishment of the corps and the situation within the first year of the establishment of the 3rd Corps was an issue which has repeatedly been addressed in the course of these proceedings. The document is obviously relevant. The probative value, the Prosecution concedes, may be not as high as other evidence but is certainly not that little that it doesn't reach the threshold of being admitted. In that respect, I may make reference to the approaches taken by other Trial Chambers, which have admitted open-source evidence and have had their views in respect to the probative value. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, would you please present these documents to the accused. But it seems, Mr. Withopf -- it seems that there is this magazine and then a list of people. Is the list part of the magazine, as an annex? There may be some mistake in the handling of documents. I'm asking you the questions, and I think we should first give you the document so that you give -- you give your view on it. The usher didn't understand, I think. First to the Prosecution and then to the accused. Mr. Withopf, in the original documents, you have the magazine, but there's also a list. I would be very surprised if the list was together with the magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If you, Mr. President, allow me a few seconds to have a closer look at the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this junction I can't give you a precise -- unfortunately, I can't give you a precise explanation what's the reason for this situation. It appears to me, however, that due to the fact that the ERN numbers indicate that the two documents weren't found together, that there is obviously some sort of a problem in handling these two obviously separate documents. I will make inquiries and at a later point in time inform the Trial Chamber accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let us show the accused all of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have to stop. First, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just about this magazine. I'd like to observe that this is not an official publication of the army or of the 3rd Corps. Probably, just judging by the title, it is a publication, a magazine which is from the -- on the same side, as it were, but it is not an official army publication. So this interview boils down to being basically just a statement by the accused, but we need to have the journalist here at the stand, take the stand to confirm that he did carry out this interview, just to confirm the existence of the interview, that it did take place, and then we could see whether we can attach any weight to the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, there was one paper left somewhere. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a very practical issue. The Prosecution, as probably Defence, would appreciate to get to know as to when the Trial Chamber intends to continue the discussion on the documents, and, of course, the Prosecution would appreciate if Defence for both accused could provide us with their lists about the documents that we discussed at any time the Trial Chamber deems appropriate. It appears to me a bit difficult to continue on Monday morning, since we have the military expert to be heard for the full week. Defence has indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: -- that they wish to examine him very extensively. So the Prosecution suggestion would be to only after General Reinhardt's testimony to continue with the discussion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Mr. Bourgon, how many documents did you have left? We'll have to stop. It's now ten to 2.00. How many documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may use this opportunity now to hand over our categories of documents so that Your Honours do have this document to take into account, if you are considering the matter over the next while. It goes category by category, and the number used, Your Honours, is the number of the contested exhibit number, the one that appears on the front of -- of each exhibit. Also, Your Honour, to indicate that at the back of this document we have attached the transcript from the 10th of February, 2004, when the Prosecution objected to a document on the basis that it was outside the time frame of the indictment. This is a matter we had raised earlier, but it's not a matter that's been addressed by the -- by the Prosecution as yet. And for the record, to indicate that Your Honours on that occasion, when the Prosecution objected, that document was not admitted into evidence; it was only marked for identification and remains so at the moment. I think there are enough copies for everyone, Your Honours. Your Honours, in addition to that, while that is being handed out, we have selected a document or two from each category. The total number of documents that we will need to go through is only ten. And, Your Honour, with your permission, I can now indicate which of those numbers we will be referring to. They are numbers which the Prosecution has already, but we have cut down from the 16 to the 10, and they are as follows: In Category A, it's two documents, number 4 and number 6; in Category B, it's number 8; in Category C, number 37 and 56; in Category D, number 28 has already been referred to by Mr. Bourgon, so there'll be no need to show the document again. All I'll require is to have a short time to make a legal submission on why a witness is required for number 28; in particular, why a witness is required for the war diaries. Number E is 54; category F is 29. On the videos, we referred to an example yesterday, number 409. It's not necessary to refer to it again. So there'll be nothing further on -- on videos. Your Honours will recall number 409 was the one regarding the establishment of the 7th Brigade where the dates were entirely different from the date of the video to the date alleged by the Prosecution in the indictment. Number H is 103; and then the final category, confusing documents. I never addressed Your Honour on this further yesterday, but there are a number of documents where we simply cannot work out how the -- the document relates from one page to the next to the translation, and there are -- there are two examples which we wish to show Your Honours, number 65 and 79, as illustrations, again, of documents which we say cannot be admitted because they just don't make sense on their face. Under "Other documents," number 57 is Colonel Stewart's testimony. The Prosecution has withdrawn that exhibit, so if number 57 can be crossed out from this list. And number 58 is the Instructions to Muslim Fighters, which I referred to yesterday. There'll be no need to look at this document, but just so Your Honours know that number 58 is that particular document, which we require a witness for. Your Honours might notice that some documents appear in more than one category, because sometimes they are contested on -- on different grounds. But when the examples are referred to, I will explain how they fit into different categories. Your Honours, I would need about 45 minutes to an hour to go through those documents at a -- at a point convenient for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Dixon. So next week we shall start with the expert witness, who's scheduled for the whole week. Should his testimony be shorter; say, should Friday be free, then straight away we could resume the hearing devoted to the documents, and we would give the floor to Mr. Bourgon so that he could present the four or five documents that are still awaiting; and then Mr. Dixon can give us some examples from the various categories using the documents that he gave the numbers of. Following this, the Chamber will issue a decision. But in the meantime, we have decided that we must have the originals, following a procedure which will be agreed between the registry and the relevant services. Before we adjourn, I turn to the Prosecution. Could the Prosecution attempt to set up an overall chart of all the documents? So those documents that have been admitted already, those that were admitted by way of a special decision, those being under discussion. But it would be organised chronologically. So you would have the first document in time up to the last document in the time frame, so that we have a full list but a chronological list with all the documents. Let me give an example: Let us assume that there is among all documents a first document dated June 1992, say. Then this document would be the first one. And the last one in the list would be dated March or April 1994. In this way, we would have the documents in their chronological order. Because you will have noticed that we have documents in folders admittedly, but there is no chronological order. Of course, this is going to represent quite a bit of work for the Prosecution, because they will have to disorder all the documents to have this list in chronological order. It hasn't been done so far, but it would be useful to have such a list. You have given us the events in chronological order; all the parties have received it. It would be good to have the same for the exhibits. And you could have a star, asterisk, for the 56 or so documents that are being contested. Or 650. Would that be a problem for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this will certainly be not a problem for the Prosecution. Such a list can be provided on short notice and within a reasonable time frame. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for the interpreters and the whole staff that had to stay and work overtime. We are going to adjourn, and I do hope to find you back here on Monday. Tomorrow is a public holiday, as you know, and then we have the weekend. So we shall resume our work with the expert witness on Monday at 4.00. Thank you -- 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of May, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
